conceptTag: Sell packaging to a food company
readerTitle: The cheaper packaging that costs a food maker more
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장 필름 공급사와 식품 제조사, 재사용 상자와 식품 유통사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: B2B 영업에서 '비싸다'는 대답은 결론이 아니다. 가격만 보는 한 사람의 점수표일 뿐이다. 구매에 관여하는 사람마다 쓰는 숫자를 찾아 총비용으로 다시 써 주면 대답이 바뀐다.
misconception: 구매 담당자가 비싸다고 하면 가격을 내리는 수밖에 없다.

sources.text: B2B 마케팅·구매 관리의 표준 개념 (구매 의사결정 집단, 총소유비용)

factChecks.note: 재사용 상자 사례(카드 7)는 수치 없이 개념만 다룹니다. 실제 수명, 세척비, 회수 운송비는 업체마다 크게 다르므로 구체적인 숫자를 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The cheaper packaging that costs a food maker more
body: You make plastic film for food packs. A snack maker runs your rival's film, and it tears on their packing line about once a week.
Your film is stronger. It's also 7.5% more per roll. The purchasing manager reads your quote and says one word: "Expensive."

image.label: A torn film roll stopping a snack packing line
image.brief: 식품 포장 라인 장면. 컨베이어 위 과자 봉지들이 멈춰 있고, 필름 롤 한 곳이 찢어져 있음. 옆에 서류를 든 구매 담당자가 가격표를 보고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고와 제품명은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Purchasing says your price is too high.
body: The purchasing manager is measured on price per roll. Your film costs $0.043 per pack. The current one costs $0.040.

options.text: Cut your price to $0.040 to match
options.feedback: You might win the order, but you give away your margin and teach the customer that your extra strength is worth nothing.

options.text: Ask who else is affected by the film, and meet them
options.feedback: This is the **buying committee** at work. Production and quality also live with the film every day, and they count different costs than purchasing does.

options.text: Send purchasing a detailed spec sheet on tear strength
options.feedback: The facts are right, but they go to the one person whose scorecard doesn't reward them. Tear strength matters most to people who never see your quote.

cards.title: Five people, five different questions.
body: A packaging decision at a food company rarely belongs to one person. Each member of the **buying committee** judges your film by a different number.
list: **Marketing:** how the pack looks on the shelf
**Finance:** the total spend for the year
cards.callout: Purchasing said no to a price. Nobody has said no to fewer line stops yet.
cards.softwareNote: Selling software to a company works the same way. The buyer sees the license fee, IT sees setup and security work, and the team using it sees hours saved. Each needs its own number.

cards.title: Count the whole cost, not the roll.
body: At one million packs a year, your film costs **$3,000 more**. The current film also causes about 50 line stops a year at $300 each, and 8,000 leaky packs worth $1.50 each. On a trial, yours cut that to 10 stops and 3,000 packs.
This is **total cost of ownership**: price plus every cost that comes with using the product.

cards.title: How do you bring the numbers back?
body: The production manager loves the trial results. But purchasing still signs the order, and their bonus is tied to unit price.

options.text: Skip purchasing and take the numbers to the plant director
options.feedback: You may win this order and lose the buyer for years. In a **buying committee**, the person you went around still has a vote next time.

options.text: Give purchasing a one-page total-cost sheet, signed off by production
options.feedback: Now purchasing can defend a higher price with **total cost of ownership** and a colleague's support. You've turned their risk into their win.

options.text: Offer a discount on another product so purchasing still shows a saving
options.feedback: It respects purchasing's scorecard, but you pay for it. A clear total-cost case might have done the same job for free.

cards.title: Your savings are only a promise.
body: A total-cost sheet built on your own estimates is easy to doubt. The numbers count only when they come from the customer's line, measured the way they measure.
Agree on the test before you run it: how many shifts, how stops are logged, who counts scrap. If the savings turn out smaller, say so. A sheet that was honest once gets believed the next time.

cards.title: Now you sell reusable crates.
body: A regional grocery distributor ships produce in single-use cardboard boxes. Your plastic crates cost many times more each but last for many trips. The warehouse manager is keen. Finance asks for the case.

options.text: Cost per trip over the crate's life, including washing and return trucking, plus less bruised produce and less waste hauling
options.feedback: This is honest **total cost of ownership**. Including washing and return costs makes the case believable to finance, the committee member most likely to check it.

options.text: A strong story about cutting cardboard waste
options.feedback: It may win over a sustainability lead, but finance asked a money question. A **buying committee** needs each member's own reason.

options.text: A big launch discount on the first order of crates
options.feedback: It shrinks the upfront price but leaves the real question open: will the crates pay back? Finance still has nothing to check.

cards.title: "Too expensive" is one person's number.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Buying committees:** find everyone who lives with the product and learn what each one measures. **Total cost of ownership:** add up price plus every cost of using it, and let the customer test the numbers.
**Try it today:** pick one business customer. List who touches your product there and the one number each of them cares about.
